title: 1st Abyss 1st Matter In Universal Questions Denial Is Worthless Against Proof

questions.question: What is the main goal of this passage at the beginning of the discussion?
questions.answer: It aims to address two major sources of doubt that weaken certainty in faith in the present age.

questions.question: How many remedies are given for escaping the first danger described in the passage?
questions.answer: Two remedies are given.

questions.question: In the first remedy, which side is described as stronger in general matters: affirmation with evidence or denial?
questions.answer: Affirmation with evidence is described as stronger.

questions.question: What example is used to show that a small number of witnesses can outweigh many deniers?
questions.answer: The example is the sighting of the new moon at the start of Ramadan.

questions.question: Why does the testimony of two people who actually saw the moon carry force?
questions.answer: Because they are affirming something based on direct observation, and their testimony supports each other.

questions.question: Why do many people saying “we did not see it” fail to overturn that proof?
questions.answer: Because not seeing something is not the same as proving it is not there.

questions.question: According to the passage, what happens when people affirm a reality on the basis of proof?
questions.answer: Their statements reinforce one another and lead toward agreement.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do deniers remain separate from one another even if they are numerous?
questions.answer: Because each denial comes from that person's own limited viewpoint and does not truly support the others.

questions.question: If one person claims something exists and another denies it, which side has the easier task of proof?
questions.answer: The one affirming it has the easier task, since a single valid sign can establish existence.

questions.question: Why is it so hard to prove total nonexistence?
questions.answer: Because it would require checking everywhere and every relevant time to rule it out completely.

questions.question: What mistake do deniers make when they judge spiritual realities?
questions.answer: They judge by their own limited perception instead of the reality itself.

questions.question: Why does the passage call the claim “it does not exist in reality” a huge falsehood in matters of belief?
questions.answer: Because such matters relate to the whole universe, so making a total denial without total knowledge is an enormous false claim.

questions.question: What issue does this passage focus on instead of repeating earlier detailed proofs?
questions.answer: It focuses on two deep sources of doubt that disturb confidence in faith today.

questions.question: The first of those sources is answered through how many main points?
questions.answer: Through two main points.

questions.question: What basic principle is taught in the first point about proving and denying?
questions.answer: A supported claim of existence is strong, while bare denial is weak.

questions.question: Which religious example is used to make that principle easy to understand?
questions.answer: The beginning-of-Ramadan moon sighting.

questions.question: In that example, why do two ordinary witnesses matter more than many respected people who did not see the moon?
questions.answer: Because actual witnessing is positive evidence, while failure to see it is only lack of personal observation.

questions.question: When several people affirm the same thing on sound grounds, how do their statements function together?
questions.answer: They back each other up.

questions.question: Why does denial not gather the same strength from numbers?
questions.answer: Because each denier is isolated within his own personal limits and obstacles.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about a person who affirms a reality?
questions.answer: That person looks beyond himself to the thing itself.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about a person who denies a reality?
questions.answer: That person often judges from his own condition rather than from full access to reality.

questions.question: If someone wants to prove that something exists, what may be enough?
questions.answer: One clear sign may be enough.

questions.question: If someone wants to prove that something has never existed anywhere, what would that require?
questions.answer: It would require an exhaustive search through all places and times.

questions.question: Why can different deniers not really form a solid united front?
questions.answer: Because the reasons they fail to perceive something differ from person to person.

questions.question: What statement can a denier honestly make about his own limitation?
questions.answer: He can say that he does not see it and therefore does not believe it.

questions.question: What stronger statement does the passage reject as false?
questions.answer: The claim that the thing does not truly exist at all.

questions.question: What summary contrast is made between affirmation and negation?
questions.answer: Affirmation is unified and mutually supporting; negation is divided and scattered.

questions.question: Why does the passage say it will not repeat a full explanation of the truth of faith here?
questions.answer: Because that fuller proof has already been established elsewhere, so this section only addresses two major sources of hesitation.

questions.question: What is the first major problem this passage tries to solve?
questions.answer: The weakness in certainty caused by denials and doubts.

questions.question: What is the first “Matter” mainly about?
questions.answer: It explains why supported affirmation is stronger than denial.

questions.question: What role does the Ramadan moon example play in the argument?
questions.answer: It gives a concrete case showing that actual sighting counts more than many people simply failing to see.

questions.question: Why is denial called weak in general questions?
questions.answer: Because it lacks direct proof and usually rests on limited non-observation.

questions.question: How does affirmation produce a kind of collective strength?
questions.answer: Different affirmations of the same truth come together and support one another.

questions.question: Why does denial fail to produce the same kind of consensus?
questions.answer: Because each denial stands alone and comes from a separate personal limitation.

questions.question: What does the passage mean by saying the affirmer judges the matter “as it is”?
questions.answer: It means he is directed toward the reality itself instead of only toward his own inability to perceive it.

questions.question: What would someone have to do to prove complete nonexistence?
questions.answer: Search all relevant places and times thoroughly enough to rule out every possibility.

questions.question: What does this show about broad denials in matters of faith?
questions.answer: It shows they make claims far beyond what human beings can actually verify.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the most a person may honestly say from limited perception?
questions.answer: That he himself does not see the thing or is not convinced by it.

questions.question: Why is a universal denial in belief-related matters treated so severely?
questions.answer: Because it claims knowledge of all reality without having such knowledge.

questions.question: What is the short final principle drawn from the first matter?
questions.answer: Positive proof is unified, while denial breaks apart into many unrelated strands.

questions.question: How does that principle answer the apparent strength of large unbelieving groups?
questions.answer: It shows that numbers alone do not make their position intellectually strong.

questions.question: At the opening of the passage, what present-day problem is being addressed?
questions.answer: The passage addresses major forms of doubt that unsettle certainty of faith.

questions.question: How is the discussion organized for escaping the first danger?
questions.answer: It is organized into two main matters.

questions.question: What does the first matter teach about the relationship between proof and denial?
questions.answer: It teaches that proof-based affirmation is strong, while denial remains weak.

questions.question: Why is the beginning-of-Ramadan moon used as an illustration?
questions.answer: Because it clearly shows that actual evidence from witnesses outweighs the mere absence of sight in others.

questions.question: Why do many denials not add up to a real proof?
questions.answer: Because each denial only reflects a person's own lack of perception, not the actual state of the matter.

questions.question: What happens when one witness points out the object to another witness in the example?
questions.answer: Their testimonies become joined and mutually confirming.

questions.question: Why can deniers not join together in the same way?
questions.answer: Because their statements come from separate barriers, not from one shared positive observation.

questions.question: What principle about nonexistence is implied by the example of searching the whole world?
questions.answer: A universal negative claim requires impossible breadth of investigation to prove.

questions.question: Why is proving existence easier than proving nonexistence?
questions.answer: Because one valid indicator can establish existence, but nonexistence would require ruling out every possibility.

questions.question: What is wrong with judging unseen realities by one’s own soul, mind, and eyesight alone?
questions.answer: It makes personal limitation the measure of reality.

questions.question: What limited claim may a person properly make from such weakness?
questions.answer: He may say he does not perceive the matter himself.

questions.question: What overreaching claim does the passage condemn?
questions.answer: The claim that the matter does not exist in reality at all.

questions.question: What conclusion is drawn about the apparent majority of deniers?
questions.answer: Their greater numbers do not give meaningful force against truth.

questions.question: What does the passage say has already been proven elsewhere, making only a shorter treatment necessary here?
questions.answer: The basic truth under discussion has already been strongly established elsewhere.

questions.question: What narrower purpose does this section then take on?
questions.answer: It focuses on two deep pits of doubt that shake confidence in faith in this age.

questions.question: In the first matter, which has more weight: positive proof or simple denial?
questions.answer: Positive proof has more weight.

questions.question: What religiously familiar example is used to explain this?
questions.answer: The sighting of the Ramadan crescent.

questions.question: In that example, why is witness-based affirmation stronger than mass denial?
questions.answer: Because seeing the moon is evidence of its presence, while not seeing it does not show its absence.

questions.question: How does affirmation lead toward consensus?
questions.answer: Each true affirmation adds support to the others.

questions.question: Why does negation fail to gain the same support from numbers?
questions.answer: Because each negation remains tied to an individual's own limits and cannot merge into one shared proof.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the viewpoint of the person who affirms?
questions.answer: He is directed toward the actual matter itself.

questions.question: What does it suggest about the viewpoint of the person who denies?
questions.answer: He is often confined within his own inability to know or see.

questions.question: What is enough to establish that something exists?
questions.answer: A single sound indication can be enough.

questions.question: What impossible burden falls on someone trying to prove absolute nonexistence?
questions.answer: He must rule out the thing everywhere and across all relevant times.

questions.question: Why can deniers not reliably strengthen one another in questions of belief?
questions.answer: Because the obstacles behind their denial differ and remain personal.

questions.question: What statement of personal limitation is treated as possible?
questions.answer: Saying that one does not see the matter and therefore does not accept it.

questions.question: What statement of objective total denial is rejected?
questions.answer: Saying that the matter does not exist in reality.

questions.question: What is the summary lesson about affirmation and negation?
questions.answer: Affirmation has one shared outcome; negation splits into many disconnected outcomes.

questions.question: What should believers not be shaken by, according to the passage?
questions.answer: They should not be shaken by the apparent size and spread of deniers.

questions.question: What does this passage choose to discuss instead of restating all the earlier proofs of faith?
questions.answer: It discusses two major causes of hesitation that disturb faith in the current age.

questions.question: How many “Matters” are offered as a way out of the first abyss of doubt?
questions.answer: Two Matters are offered.

questions.question: What central claim does the First Matter make about denial?
questions.answer: It says denial is very weak when facing a proven affirmation in general matters.

questions.question: Which example from Muslim life is used to make this point understandable?
questions.answer: The example of seeing the new moon that marks the start of Ramadan.

questions.question: Why do two ordinary people who actually saw the moon outweigh many scholars who did not?
questions.answer: Because direct witness establishes presence, while failure to notice something does not establish absence.

questions.question: What happens to separate affirmations when they concern the same reality?
questions.answer: They come together and strengthen one another.

questions.question: Why is there no comparable unity among denials?
questions.answer: Because each denial arises from a separate person's own lack of knowledge or perception.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the difference between how an affirmer and a denier approach the matter?
questions.answer: The affirmer attends to the reality itself, while the denier often stays trapped in his own perspective.

questions.question: If someone claims a thing exists, how might he prove it?
questions.answer: He may prove it with a single clear indication.

questions.question: If someone claims a thing never existed at all, what would he need to do?
questions.answer: He would need complete investigation across the whole world and all past times.

questions.question: Why is a sweeping denial in belief-related questions beyond human ability to verify?
questions.answer: Because those questions involve realities wider than any person can fully survey.

questions.question: What kind of statement about one's own perception does the passage allow?
questions.answer: A person may honestly say he does not see or recognize the matter.

questions.question: What stronger statement is judged false in such cases?
questions.answer: Declaring that the matter does not exist in actual reality.

questions.question: What concise distinction is made between affirmation and negation after this discussion?
questions.answer: Affirmation is one and mutually supportive; negation is many and fragmented.

questions.question: What conclusion follows about the visible majority of those who reject belief?
questions.answer: Their numerical strength does not amount to true evidential strength.
